newsitem.title: FRANCE: France details capital injections planned in 1996.
newsitem.headline: France details capital injections planned in 1996.

text.p: The French government plans to spend funds set aside for capital injections this year mainly on recapitalising Thomson SA and funding defeasance structures -- shell companies set up to manage hived off loans --for state bank Credit Lyonnais and property lender Comptoir des Entrepreneurs, Finance Minister Jean Arthuis said on Thursday.
Thomson is due to have an 11 billion franc capitalisation before it is sold to Lagardere Groupe.
Arthuis told reporters the government would also have to spend 2.9 billion francs buying Credit Lyonnais shares in Thomson.
One billion would be needed for state-owned film studio Societe Francaise de Production (SFP), which the government aims to privatise before the end of the year.
Another 2.5 billion francs were needed to pay for a managed wind-down of property lender Credit Foncier, Arthuis said.
The rest would go to fund defeasance structures of Credit Lyonnais and Comptoir des Entrepreneurs.

The government has some 23 billion francs to spend between now and the end of the year on recapitalisations, which are financed through privatisations of state-owned companies and from central government budget funding.
The government said on Wednesday its sale of a stake that day in oil company Elf Aquitaine brought total revenues from privatisations this year to 27 billion francs.
On top of the 27 billion francs in privatisation receipts available for capital injections this year, a total 8.7 billion is also to be provided from central government budget funds.
A total of 13 billion francs has already been spent on capital injections this year, going to Air France, arms maker GIAT, regional bank Societe Marseillaise de Credit and Cie Generale Maritime.

"That leaves 23 billion francs which will therefore be shared out between now and the end of the year between companies which need to be recapitalised, particularly those that are in the course of being privatised," Budget Minister Alain Lamassoure said on Wednesday.
